blocks.x: I got it on now. We moved the microphone a little bit, so, because with that Cajun blood, you might talk with your hands a little too much.
Well, you want to give it a test now and see how the...
Sure, yeah, we got the second reel on.
Everything is working all right now?
Yeah, it's better than ever. Let me give a listen to it.
Testing one, two, three, four, five. How's this old Cajun coming out now?
Except it came out in English. So your very first job was with Joseph Salvaggio, and you say it was something like Lombardo style.
It was a Lombardo type band, Dick.
Did he ever have a mellophone?

No, but we had a boy that played the bass horn, like Lombardo has. And after four hour rehearsals two or three times a week, one year later, it really sounded great. We really, then we began getting jobs on a West End roof, and spot jobs. We all had things to do in a day, so we couldn't take steady work. We were a bunch of kids. And it really sounded good. It's just that after three years, I was ready to make a move to play a different type of music. With all due respect to the Lombardo type of music, I loved it, but I wanted to play something with more of a lift, you know. That's why I moved to the Blue Parody in the hopes of someday getting with Al Streaming.
What did Salvaggio play?

He's a very fine piano player. Very fine pianist. He still plays. He's around still playing. His brother played lead alto sax and clarinet. I don't know if the brothers playing sax and clarinet any more, but Joe, the leader of the group, was a very fine musician.
Do you remember his brother's name?

Yeah. Philip. Philip Salvaggio. And he was a very fine sax player. How many reads did he have in the band? We had three saxes. Three saxes. And we had trumpet and trombone and guitar, or banjo, and bass horn, and Joe on piano.
Who played tenor in the band?

Well, we went through two or three different tenor men. George Perkins, who's passed away since, the late George Perkins, who was a very fine tenor man. He was one of the tenor men. And at another time we had a boy by the name of Jack DeShari. He was a very fine tenor man. I think Jack has since passed away too.
And third alto? And third alto?

I don't recall who was on third alto. Like I say, Dick, we had several, during the four years we went through changes, you know. We probably had two or three different men on third alto also. I can't remember.
And what about the...

I think Jack DeShari played third alto, because George Perkins played tenor. And Philip played lead alto sax and clarinet. And on trumpet? And on bass horn we had a very fine audition by the name of John Pudra. I don't know if he's still in town or whether he's still around or what, but John Pudra was a very fine bass horn player.
There was a composer by that name, but I think he must have been older than that man.

Well, I would say John Pudra today would be in his around middle fifties, fifty-five, fifty-six, maybe fifty-eight, fifty-seven. Well, let's see. If he was still living. I think he must be, I think they moved out of town, I'm not sure. But John Pudra was a very fine bass player. Well you were playing... Bass horn player. Yeah.
If the crash was October of twenty-nine.
I think it was October twenty-nine. Yeah, it was.
Late October. I don't remember it too well myself. But anyway, Salvatio, were you with him when the crash hit or not?

No. No, I went with him after things dwindled down and all that, after that three or four months of working day and night. Then I went with my first group. Then I was approached by a friend of mine to join this first group that had been organized for about two months, the Salvatio group, because they needed a guitar or banjo.
So when the crash came, you knew something about the banjo, enough to be able to... Well, I was practicing, you know. Yeah, and you could cut it with Salvatio.
Yeah, I was going through that dollar book that I bought with all those chords. Yeah, well. Even though I didn't have too much time to practice.
Yeah. So anyway, back to the line up in the band. He had one or two trumpets.
He had one trumpet. Yeah. Just one trumpet and I think one trombone. If I remember right, we had an eight piece band. I don't think we had a nine piece band. Let's see. An eight piece band.
And do you remember the trumpet player, the trombone player, any of them?

Well, we had different trumpet players that went through in that three or four years. Even Rene LeWap went through it for a while. Oh. Your current day popular Rene LeWap who plays all these carnival balls and does a wonderful job. Rene went through it for several months, maybe six or eight months. I don't recall how long each man stayed. A young fine trumpet man by the name of Walter Darwin played trumpet with us for a while and he was I think pretty active in the Lions Club lately or in the last few years. I haven't seen Walter in many years. But last time I saw him I think he was active in the Lions Club. He was a fine little trumpet man. I remember we going way back to 1929 or early 30. So I think that's the only two trumpet men I can recall but there were two or three others but I can't recall their names. It was too far back there.
And the trombone players you don't remember?

No. Well, we had, I don't know if, yeah, a boy by the name of Chatelaine played trombone with us at one time. Uh, I can't recall the others but there was probably one, maybe one other one. And a drummer?
A drummer. Did you tell me or not?

No, I can't recall who was on drums because we went through one or two drummers too. Yeah, well. Drummers and, uh, drummers I can't recall. Chatelaine was on trombone. Were you in the union then? Oh no, this is way before the union. We never joined the union until, uh, I think around 1939 I was with Al Streeman.
Uh huh.

And we joined the union, Dick, when the hotels went closed shop, which I think was around 1939. Uh huh. And Streeman used to get all the work in town, like I told you before. Uh huh. In the early years with Streeman, we were getting work 25, 26 nights a month.
Uh huh.

And we were non-union and we were making more than union scale. And that was the reason we didn't join a union. We didn't have to join a union. The union was actually jealous of us that we were making that amount of money. And they offered us into the union three different times. And I used to think Al Streeman was kidding me.
Uh huh.

But until he showed me the letter that the union wanted us in and offered the whole group in for nothing without any initiation fee or anything. Uh huh. And we didn't go. And, and in 39 when the unions went, uh, the hotels all went closed shop, which meant that you had to be union to play in any hotel. Uh huh. When we began losing work, you know, because we were playing for big oil companies and sororities and fraternities and what have you. Uh huh. And nearly all your work was in hotels. So I told Al, I said, Al, why don't you call a meeting at your house and talk it over with the fellas in the band? And I said, let's join a union. And talk about joining a union. I said, you're losing all your good work, all your two lane work. You played for all these, uh, Rush Week, you'd get all this work. And two lane fraternities besides regular, sororities, fraternities. And in the old days, they, they were more fraternity and sorority dances than they are nowadays. Man, every week, every two weeks, every month there were sorority dances. Now they give them once a year. It's nothing like the old days. There was plenty parties in the old days. Of course, the economy I guess has a lot to do with that. Everything is so high now. You know, that's the reason why, you know, I have a sorority dance every month now. I dance at the other, in the tea room every week like they used to have. There was a lot of work for musicians in the old days. And there's still a lot of work, but I mean it's a whole different situation nowadays. But the price is the way they are, you know.
Did you ever play a job on guitar with Salvaggio?
I think the last year I switched over on guitar.
Yeah, I got that straight. I hope, anyway. Yeah. Then the Blue Parody you were playing? I was playing guitar. Guitar the whole time. Yeah.

I was only with Blue Parody four months now. Four months, yeah. When I had an opportunity to go with Streaming. So I grabbed that opportunity and I went with Streaming. Because they had a tremendous group. Not that the Blue Parody didn't, they had a good group too. But I knew a lot of the guys in the Streaming band and I really enjoyed working with that group besides the fact they got a tremendous amount of work. Why did you switch to guitar?
Do you know?
Well, because in 1932, guitarists sort of became real popular and banjos started dying down.
Now banjos are back again.

Yeah. To prove it, I'll tell you one thing which I always regretted. I had a good banjo which I said I bought second hand for $75. And after I played the banjo for those number of years, as I mentioned before, and I went to Whirlines and I traded in my banjo on a stake string guitar, a good Epiphone guitar. Whirlines gave me $25 on that banjo. If I had that banjo today I could sell it for $500.
What kind was it?

It was a Paramount banjo. You see banjos came back in the late years and became real popular. But between 28 and 32 banjos were popular and then around 32, nearly everybody played banjos, switched to six string guitar and banjos dwindled down slightly for a few years. So in order to keep up with the times I got me a six string guitar and started working on that. And then when I bought my string bass in 37 at Whirlines, I said well I'm not going to make that mistake again. I put that six string guitar under the bed in a plush line case that I bought at Whirlines. And I said I'm going to leave that under the bed and when my daughters get old enough maybe they'll want to play it. You see? I wasn't going to go to Whirlines and get $25 on that. So you know that bass laid under that bed in that case for 12 years and the daughters never did get interested in playing that because I said before one studied clarinet and got the scholarship to a Dominican high school. And then years later they both studied piano. So then my wife says Bob why don't you sell your guitar, the kids are not going to fool with it. So I put an ad in the paper and I sold a guitar for $125 to a friend of mine who had a guitar exactly like it and he had dropped it and cracked it. So I got to earn $25 for the guitar. Who was it that bought it?
A professional musician?
Yeah, a musician friend of mine by the name of Larry Vecca who recently passed away, I think he passed away two or three years ago. He had his own band.
Yeah from a famous family too. Larry Vecca.
His father played with Jack Lane. He's a Vecca also that plays piano. He used to work at the Times for Keown. He's related to Larry Vecca.
I've never met any of them but Jack Lane used to talk about the Lawrence who was the father
I guess. Yeah. Larry Vecca. Well Larry used to have a big nine, ten, twelve piece band and he operated for many years. And he, my friend, he saw the ad in the paper he came up and grabbed the guitar.
How did you get interested in bass by the way?

Well I always did like bass. I always did like string bass, Dick. And around 1937 after playing the guitar for four years in the band I decided, well you know the bass player with the Al Streaming Band who was the vice president of the Soil Company and had to do all that road traveling. He was told Streaming and he said, Al I'm going to have to quit the band. He said, I got too much traveling. He had been with the band ten years. So he left the band and that's when Al told me, he said, Bob why don't you switch over to bass? I know you just recently bought one and you've been working out at the house with it. And because when I bought the guitar I didn't know whether to buy a bass or a guitar. So I bought the guitar and I said, well maybe later on if I still like bass I'll get me a string bass. So four years later in 1937, an early 37, because I already had the bass when I got married in October. So it must have been an early 37 and I bought the string bass at Whirlands. And I bought this bass method book and taught myself as much as I could about it and still be able to work in the daytime, which I was still in those brokerage houses. See I went to work in my first brokerage house in 1928 and I spent seven years with them. And they, they were John F. Clark and Company and they consolidated with the E.A. Pearson Company. And the E.A. Pearson Company consolidated with Fenner and Bean. Then Fenner and Bean consolidated with Merrill Lynch, Pierce Fenner, Ungolight and Smith and all that business, which is now your Merrill Lynch, you know, the big deal. But anyway, I left after, now we're strictly talking about the day job. After seven years with Clark, we went over to Fenner and Bean. I was with Fenner and Bean, excuse me, with Fenner and Bean over a few years when I decided to take a government examination. So I took about six government examinations, some that I wasn't even qualified to take. And I passed three or four of them. And then I got a government offer and that's when I went to work for the War Department down to the Port of Embarcation. And I was there one year when Pearl Harbor came along and then three months to the day after Pearl Harbor, I joined the Navy, stayed in the Navy five years. And I didn't play music for five years, Dick. I could have joined the Navy as a musician, but I'd been playing music and working in the day for thirteen years and I figured I'm going to give it a rest for a while. I played four or five times during that five years up in the US. So that's about the only time I played music. And I think we had a few jam sessions at guys' houses, you know. So if I played ten times in five years, I played plenty, you know. And then after I got out of the Navy in 47, I was streaming, held my job open for a while. So I went back. He had used a lot of substitutes. And I went back with Al. And I stayed with Al from 47 to 56. And in 53, I went with Gerard and the famous Doe, but I worked there three nights a week and worked with Streaming three nights a week. Until 56 when Al Hurts says, Bob, why don't you quit your day job and come work with me? And that brings that up to date then.
But why does Treeman want you on bass? Do you know?

Well, he knew I had a bass at the house that I'd been working out on. Because I told him when I bought the bass, I said, I bought me a string bass, Al. I'm practicing at the house. And I had no idea that the bass player was ever going to quit. And he was a good friend of mine, a fine bass player. I knew he worked for an oil company, you know. But I just bought the bass because I liked the bass. That's all. And I wanted to try to learn the bass. I had a job. I wasn't worrying about the job. I was playing guitar in the band. I wasn't trying to take nobody's job.
I was trying to take a job. Yeah. No, I just can't figure out why he wanted you on bass on that particular instrument rather
than guitar. Well, I guess he thought he would give me an opportunity to play the bass. Oh, yeah. Because he knew I had one and was practicing at the house.
Well, what's the foundation of a band? That's what I'm really getting at.
Well, I think the foundation of a band? Drum, bass, and piano. That's your foundation. That's what gives it its depth.

I don't know. I think it was Bill Cray, somebody like that, or Leonard Ferguson, one of the guys, musicians that I've talked to, saying that all nightclub owners want to get rid of bass. They don't understand the importance of it, you know. No, I don't. And he was saying how important the bass is.

I don't agree with that. Not all nightclubers want to. I'll tell you where you might have misunderstood them. It's not the nightclub owners want to get rid of the bass. It's because to a band leader, your drum, bass, and piano are three important instruments. You're a foundation. We're supplying the bottom, and we're giving it the drive and the depth. And where you may have gotten the wrong opinion, usually when the unions raise the scale on these steady band leaders, and you have a six-piece band, and they're playing six nights a week and one night off, which we have to have because of union rules. And every time the union votes a raise every year, every other year, something like that, and you have a six-piece band in this club, well, I think most of the time out of Spike, the club owners just for Spike will cut the band down to five men. And they usually either cut out the trombone or the bass, but they don't tell the band leader who to cut out. They'll say, we're going to cut you down to five men, just to save those few dollars because of the raise. And then three or four months later, they usually bill it back to six men again. But I sometimes think they do it for Spike, because it's the musicians that's making the money for them. We're bringing in their profits. Oh, yeah. And they seem to realize that months later, they're back to six men again.
Well, some people just don't appreciate what good time is, either.

Now, some band leaders, some band leaders let the trombone player go. Now, that was the case with The Last Straws when we went to Famous Goat some time back. They cut all three bands down. At the Famous Store right now, we have three bands, seven days a week, all year round, seven nights a week. First band comes on at 12, 15 to 5. We have the middle shift now. We used to have the night shift for many years. In fact, this is the first time in my life. I get home at 10.30 at night. Now, I'm used to getting home at 3 or 4 o'clock in the morning. First band comes on at 12, 15 to 5. Now, we come on at 5, 15 to 10. This third band comes on at 10, 15 to 3. Now, that's seven days a week. Now, we have a relief band that plays three nights a week there, relieving us on our day or night off, because we have to have a day or night off. We can only work six days or nights a week. And getting back to what I wanted to say, when they had cut the band down to five men, about a year ago, when I was with Nicky's Last Straws, we had six men there. I was there eight months with Nicky's Last Straws. They decided to cut down to five men. So they cut all three bands down to five men. And so they let the bass go. Well, I was home three weeks when they decided to let the trombone go. They missed the bass more than the trombone. Mm-hmm. So I went back to work. And that's when I went with the Tony Mitchell group. They called me back. Did they let Nicky go? No, no. Nick Gagliotti. No. They had let a bass horn player go with the Tony Mitchell group. Oh, I see. He was playing bass horn, I think. No, trombone. He was playing trombone with the Tony Mitchell group. And so they decided that they wanted the bass instead of the trombone. So that's when I joined the Tony Mitchell group. You see, Mitchell and Nicky were playing at the door. Two different bands.
And now they have different bands. Now there's three five piece bands there now.

You have Tony Mitchell. Tony Mitchell and the Famous Door Five. And you have Thomas Jefferson and his Creole Jazz Band. And at night you have, well, in the midst of a change right now, Jim LaRocca's going in at night now. Tommy Yedda was there at night, but he left. And Jim LaRocca is related to Nick LaRocca in some way. I don't know whether he's son or uncle, one or the other. He's son. And what about Jimmy Isle? Where is he? Jimmy Isle moved down to the Maison Bourbon. He has the early shift there. They work 11.30 to 4. Yeah. The second band comes on from 4 to 9. Who's got the second band now? Oh yeah, Howard Hollis Camus. Yes, I know him. Hollis Camus, who's an albino, plays clarinet, plays real fine clarinet and tenor sax. Hollis Camus, and he's a Cajun band, he calls it, I think. They're there from 5 to 9. And from 9 to 1 or 1.30, you have Lou Saino. Lou Saino is at the Maison Bourbon now. So they have three bands there. They have three bands at the Famous Door. And you have two bands at the Blue Angel. the Blue Angel. the Blue Angel. the Blue Angel. the Blue Angel.
The third reel is on now Bob.
Alright. Okay. How's the volume and the meters we're reading?
Well what's your name? Say it again.
Uh, this is Bob Coquille being interviewed by Dick Alling at the Jazz Al-Kyfe.
It's working fine.
That's good.

You know, when I asked you about the mellophone I wanted to mention to you was it uh, uh, how do you call it? Uh, Dudley Fosdick used to play mellophone with Lombardo. And there are very few hot mellophone players that I ever knew in my life. And I just wondered how many you knew who played mellophone around town.

I don't recall seeing it but you said he played it with a lombardo band. Now he may have had it on the side. He might have played trumpet and mellophone, which I've seen happen. Yeah. In fact the late Monk Hable was the drummer at the famous store for many years. And Monk had an old mellophone on the side which he picked up and played a beautiful jazz chorus on. Oh yeah. If you ever heard of that, I don't know if you know about that.

Oh sure, well I knew Monk. He was the first jazz musician in New Orleans that I ever got to know was Monk. And that was when he was working on Broadway in the Alcohol Factory. Right. Walking around in it all day long.

You know Dick, I really feel very good of having had the opportunity of working with fellas like the late Monk Hable, the late Larry Shields, and Jeff Riddick, and the late Almond Hug. Which Shields? Larry Shields. Harry Shields.
Harry, yeah.

Harry, yeah. Larry is his brother who passed away many years ago. Now Larry, the one that was in California, he wrote clarinet, marmalade, plus many other tunes. Oh. No, I'm talking about having had the pleasure of working with the late Monk Hazel, the late Harry Shields, and the late Almond Hug, and of course the late Sharky's. I feel really honored having had the opportunity of working with guys like that. And of course I really enjoyed working with Al Hurd and Pete Fountain, and of course Bob Havens and all those jazz greats. And of course Raymond Boyk, who I have a lot of respect for. And Tony Mitchell, I can't leave Tony out. Tony's a marvelous musician, marvelous clarinet player. And you know who I think is a very fine trumpet man? It's Jim LaRocka. I love Jim LaRocka's playing. He's a powerhouse like Al Hurd.
I haven't heard him in years.

Jim is, and I understand he's coming back in the famous store. He's gonna take over the group that's on a night shift, which was formerly Tommy Yedda's group. You know, Tommy Yedda left about a month ago. And I'm glad to see Jim LaRocka come back. He plays a lot of trumpet. To me, he's one of the finest young trumpet men around. He's a powerhouse, I tell you.
There's so many that I like, and so many that it seems to me never really gone places. For example, I enjoy Connie Jones' playing.
I love Connie Jones' playing.
And he knows tunes like, I'll Be a Friend with Pleasure. One day I just wanted to bug him and I asked him for that. He knew it.

What I like about Connie Jones is not only his marvelous playing, but like you just mentioned, he plays a lot of tunes, good old Dixieland tunes, that a lot of the other Dixieland bands don't play. Oh yeah. And that's what I enjoyed the year working with Sharky's Dixieland band, with the old Sharky's Kings of Dixieland. I enjoyed that year with Sharky because Sharky played a lot of good old Dixieland tunes that I had not played with any of the other groups. Even when I was with Al Hurd or the late George Arrod, who I have a world of respect for the late George Arrod. Oh yeah. I couldn't wait to get to work at night to play with George. He had so much front line personality and such good tone quality on that trumpet. He played like Ray Anthony, man. He had beautiful tone quality. And as I mentioned before, the late George Arrod could make the audience laugh, he could make them cry, he could make it so quiet in that famous store where you'd hear pin drop. And he would imitate Jimmy Durante, he would imitate Libby Rache, he would imitate Sam Butera. He would imitate anybody, and just have the audience in stitches. I tell you, he was really a marvelous musician. And we were really all sad when he passed away because Blaze D'Antoni, I don't know if you heard of Blaze D'Antoni, wanted George Arrod to go to Las Vegas. And he wanted George to go for three months. I was playing with the band then. And George says, well I don't want to leave Hip Ginley that long to go to Vegas because Hip has been too nice to me. Hip had the famous dope. And it was decided that there was to be no option because he didn't want to go there for three months with an option to stay longer. He didn't want to leave Hip any longer. And then George came down with a cancer surgery before he could ever get away from the famous dope. And it was a known fact that he had about a year to live. And we had all made excuses to George on the side that we couldn't go. We made some kind of excuse that we couldn't go to Vegas for this reason or that reason. Because if we would have gone to Vegas, the man would have killed himself in three months instead of a year. And I know the musicians in the band would verify that station. We all made excuses. Because we wanted to keep George as long as we could. Because that's how great a musician we thought he was. He was a great loss to the music world.
I remember when he had that examination and everything. It just sounded hopeless from what Johnny Wiggs told me. Johnny I think was the one who told me about it. It was a shock.

Because, you know, George was so full of life. Oh, he was tremendous. Tremendous. I couldn't wait to get to work at night. I was getting three hours sleep a night in those days. Because in those days we were at the night shift. We would work nine or three and we'd be alternating with the Dukes of Dixieland or some other group like that or with Santa or some group, I don't recall. But at nine or three I'd get home at 315 or 320 and I had to get up at six and go to work to get ready to go to work because I had to be at work at seven o'clock. And I did that for three years.
Did you get a nap in the afternoon?

Yeah, I'd take a nap in the afternoon when I got home for about an hour and a half before I went to work. But I couldn't get to work. I couldn't wait to get to work with Gerard. Yeah. I enjoyed it that much.
You know, I never have known much about the Blue Parody except those brothers.

Well, they had a nine piece dance band and they had a good group. It was a good group, but Stremend had just a little better group. They played with a little more drive and of course they were getting three times more work than the Blue Parody. But the Blue Parody had a good group. They got work, but they didn't get as much as Stremend.
Who was in the Blue Parody?

Oh, I can't remember all the fellas. Well, Angelo was on trumpet. He was the band leader. A fellow on drums was a CPA nowadays. Phillip Quaglina was on trombone. Joe Quaglina was on third alto or first alto. I don't recall which one. A boy by the name of S.J. Coogan who worked for the federal government many years later. He was on saxophone, probably tenor sax I guess. Maybe he played lead alto. S.J. Coogan played lead alto. Joe Quaglina probably played lead a third, I don't recall which. And I can't remember. Johnny somebody was on drums. That's the guy that was a CPA later in the years. And I was on guitar, I wasn't on bass and I was still on six string guitar. I can't recall, I can't remember who was on piano. That's too far back.
Yeah, and you had, did he have one or two trumpets? What did they have?

Well if it was an eight piece band he had one trumpet and he had one trombone. If you had a nine piece band they would add another trumpet. You would have two trumpets and a trombone. So it really depended on the work, on the engagement. If you had a nine piece booking you would have three brass. You would have first trumpet, second trumpet and trombone. And you would add a second trumpet.
And who was the bass horn player that you were playing? Did we get his name or do you?
I can't remember who was on bass with Blue Parity because I was only with that group four months. What kind of a? But they had a good group, it was a good band. What did they get?
Did they get spots or sticks? You know I was fortunate.
Every band I ever played with was a good band. I can't put any band down. I was very fortunate.
Yeah, well I don't like to put bands down. I will say I don't like to go on Bourbon Street but that's not anybody's fault really. Well Bourbon Street is all tourist trade.
There's 99% tourist trade.

Yeah. I sneak around and listen to you on the side. It's just, it's too expensive. The tourists can afford that, really. That's right. But when you're with bands like Salvaggio and the Blue Parity, would they have any steady work at all? All spots? All spots.
No, we weren't interested in steady work. We didn't want to work six nights a week. Yeah. Because we all had day jobs, you know, in those days.
And would that be house parties, dances, fraternities, sororities?

House parties, sororities. Sororities and fraternities. That was the main thing in the old days, Dick. Like I told you before. In the old days, in the 30s, in the late 20s and 30s, maybe up to, maybe up to 40. Between 28 and 40, 1940. There were many sorority and fraternity dances. Plenty of them. Sororities used to give a dance at least once a month. And fraternity is the same way, at least once a month. Some maybe twice a month. Used to be able to go to the Audubon Tea Room every Sunday there was a dance at the Audubon Tea Room. Which has since burned down.
Yeah.
I think they were going to build another one, I don't know.
Sure.

But that's in the olden days. And you all, they had, and of course you played for conventions, there was always conventions coming up and they would hire various groups, various small groups or big groups. But most of our work in the old days, the way we operated, was sororities and fraternities and clubs and house parties and things like that. Which there were plenty of, more of then than you have now.
That's from the beginning up to the time you joined the Navy.

Right, right. And then after the war, things seemed to change. They were less, they weren't quite as often. There may be the sorority fraternities might be every six months instead of every month. And now I've seen some of them, they give one party a year now, or one banquet a year or something like that, or maybe some of them still give quarterly or twice a year, every six months.
Well, when you played these jobs, would anybody ever have an MC or anything like that?

Well, in the old days, quite often we'd play for a big dance in the tea room and there'd be five acts of floor shows. We'd have to play for the five acts of the floor show. I don't know if you remember the late Emil Parra. Oh yeah. I sang for years and years at Pat O'Brien's. I knew him there. Emil Parra. Well, let me tell you, Emil Parra was always an MC and he was one of the greatest MCs in New Orleans that I've ever seen. And every time we had five acts of floor shows, a play after the dance, or maybe during the middle of the party they'd put on five acts of shows, you know, girl dancers or whatever, you're a magician or whatever have you. Well, Emil Parra always had the job of being the MC for the floor show. This was before he went to Pat O'Brien's, now this is way back. And Emil was a marvelous dancer and marvelous MC. And he used to always wind up his act by getting on top of the baby grand piano and jumping way up in the air and almost landing on his back. I used to get scared to death every time he did that. But he'd never miss. And he was so full of vim, vigor, and vitality. He was personality plus. That's why he was later hired at Pat O'Brien, where he remained for years until he passed away.
Did he? He must have been in the 50s when he passed. I would imagine that around the time. Somewhere around that time.
I would imagine that around the time. Somewhere around that time.
Anyway, he'd jump off the top of the piano and he'd land on the piano or the floor. And not only jump off the piano.

When he jumped off the piano, I don't care if it was an upright or a baby grand, he would jump up in the air three or four feet down to the dance floor and, you know, land his back would miss the floor that much, you know, like two inches. And he'd never miss. And it used to frighten me to death every time he did that. And he'd just pop right up on his feet? Pop right up. Oh, he was a good athlete, I guess. And a marvelous dancer.
See, I never saw him do any of that. All I ever saw him do was sing and dance.

He was about the best MC in New Orleans that I've seen during my career, you know. Did he ever tell any jokes? No, but he knew how to talk to people. He knew how to get people to liven up a party. He was never at a loss for words, let's put it that way.
Yeah.

He was like this with his talk. He wouldn't give people a chance to say no or anything, man. I mean, they were out on the floor. If nobody was dancing quick enough, Emile would have been dancing in five minutes. He just full of that vim, vigor and vitality, plus personality, plus. And he knew how to liven up the deadest party you ever saw. He could liven it up in five minutes.
He must have been on the day. And he did great at Pat O'Brien's.

He was a real asset at Pat O'Brien's. And, you know, being at Pat O'Brien's all those years. Now, of course, Emile had traveled all over the country before he ever come down here. Emile was very popular. And working all those years at Pat O'Brien's, Emile knew every college song in the United States. I don't think there was any college song in the United States that Emile didn't know the words to. And he was about the only one in New Orleans that could really sing all the college songs that I knew of.
Well, do you think he wasn't from New Orleans? No, I think he was from New Orleans. Yeah, but he traveled.
He did extensive traveling before all of that. Yeah, he did a lot of traveling.
He once told me he was a Creole. But that could mean, you know, you could be from another place and be a Creole. Probably so. I would imagine he's from New Orleans.

He lived up in Carrollton somewhere. I even remember that it was Carrollton. I couldn't point out the house, but he lived in Carrollton. That was another great loss to the end of the year. He was a great loss to the entertainment field. He had such great, he was like Gerard. He had so much personality. Yeah.
Well, George, certainly one thing that people used to talk about with him was his drive, too, the musicians. He played with tremendous drive.
Yeah. He played with tremendous drive.
I can remember.
I only caught one recording with George, and I was on Good Time Jazz label. And the late Doc Souchon was in charge of that recording session.
Yeah, we have it here. I played it the other day.

And there was, I think, four bands on that recording. And we only played three tunes. Dr. Jazz, Sand, and Liebestrown. We played those three numbers. But it was a pleasure working with George at that famous tour every night. I really enjoyed it. Well, he had a hit with Liebestrown, didn't he?
I don't know.
I think at one point he had a single out, but somebody did at that point.
I know. He featured that kind of trumpet that he played. He played so fine. I really enjoyed it.

He had such good tone quality, and like you said before, he played a lot of drive. Well, did you have any sync? He used to do such a beautiful job on tunes like Melancholy Rhapsody. I couldn't wait to hear it every night.
Because he made that with the Basin Street Six. Yeah, right. Which, how did that one too?

I'd like to get another copy of that little, you know, I just cracked my little EP on that Basin Street Six. Oh, really? That Melancholy Rhapsody. I cracked my little 45 on that. And I don't think I'm going to be able to get another one.
Well, Harvey Rubin may be able to make a, or Laz Muscat may be able to make you a copy, because they've got all the equipment hooked up to copy deals.
Well, I have it on, I have it on a cassette. Yeah, that's what I'm talking about. I have it on a cassette. But my little 45 that I made my cassettes from, I cracked my 45.

Yeah, well the cassettes never sounded as good to me. I was really disappointed. Yeah, I always like to hear the original if I can. Sure. Well, uh, was there any band that the Blue Parody in particular modeled itself on, or?
No, in fact, like I said before, the Blue Parody had a group, a good group. It was only out of the streaming group.
Mm-hmm. But did they have an arranger, or did they buy stocks, or?

No, no, it was all stocks and a few specials. Just like streaming operated. Mm-hmm. Streaming operated with 80% stock arrangements and about 20% of special arrangements. Streaming would have 10 or 12 special arrangements, maybe more. Or used to order them out of New York, you know. And Blue Parody was the same way. They played a lot of stocks and a few specials. Well, who did the singing? Oh. In the streaming band we had various singers. Helen, I'm trying to think of her last name. She was Miss New Orleans at one time. Yeah. And she left to sing with the Larry Clinton band. She sang with Al Stringer. Helen Englade, I was trying to think of her last name, who of course has since married and all that. But I think she won the Miss New Orleans contest, I believe, at one time. And she sang, and she later left with the Larry Clinton band. She traveled with Larry Clinton, I think she later married a man out of the Larry Clinton band, a sax player. And Jane Villegas sang with the Al Stringer band for a good while. Jane Villegas, her sister was Margaret Villegas. She just passed away recently. And Margaret Villegas was a professional singer who sang with some name bands, the George Hall band, big band, you know, traveled around the country. She sang under the name of Loretta Lee. And that was her kid sister Jane Villegas who used to sing with us. And the trumpet player that played, that I had the pleasure of working with, Irving Dusan, he's president of Columbia Homestead right now. It was a marvelous trumpet player. And I had the pleasure of working with Irving, with the Al Stringer band, for at least eight of the nineteen years he played with Al Stringer, a marvelous trumpet player.
Did he sing?

No, he didn't sing, but he played a driving trumpet. He married Loretta Lee. I see. This professional singer who sang with George Hall and many named bands around the country. Her name was Margaret Villegas, and she just recently passed away within the last six, eight months of it.
I, I, I, I'm curious whether they added a, well you know they called them boy singers and girl singers in. Would they add any boy singers? Well they call them vocalists, so.

Yeah. They're vocalists, I guess. Now, Irving Dusan who was presently president of Columbia Homestead, gave up playing trumpet, he's president of Homestead. He has a brother who is an attorney, Edward Dusan. Now he played fine trumpet also. He was with Al Stringer band, had the pleasure of working with him four or five years with the Al Stringer band. He's doing very little playing now. I doubt if he's playing at all, because he's a very busy attorney nowadays. All those fellas, I understand at one time, I don't know how true it is, but I understand Louis Primer even spent two years with Al Stringer. I don't know if that's true or not. I was told that.
It could be before you joined.

A lot of fine musicians went through the Al Stringer band, because Al Stringer had a band, I never joined his group until 1933, and I think he started out around 1923, about ten years ago. He had a good band. And he used to play every night in a room called the Venetian Room, the Roosevelt from 6.30 to 8.30. And the Venetian Room is right where the Blue Room is right now. He played in there every night from 6.30 to 8.30, and they had a broadcast, which used to get them up in Canada. Every night they broadcast half hour. And every night after that 6.30 to 8.30, they had a spot job every night, 26, 28 nights a month. So you know they were real popular.
How did they broadcast from there? How did they hook up at the radio station? Oh, WWL. WWL, I guess.
Yeah.
Must have been if it got to Canada, because that was clear channeling. It was definitely WWL.

Yeah. And Charlie Hardesty, he used to sing with the band. He was the drummer with Alice Freeman in the old days. Of course, in the first few years when I was with the band, too. And Charlie had a marvelous voice. And he was with the band a long time, and we used to get letters from Canada. It was definitely WWL, because that was a 50,000-watt job that carried way up there.
